content_metadata.description: A news segment discussing the introduction of ten new bills in New York State aimed at tightening gun laws. The segment includes interviews and discussions about the impact of these laws.

qAndA.answer: Raise the age for buying semi-automatic rifles to 21, tighten existing red flag laws, outlaw the sale of body vests, make mass casualty threats a crime, and create a task force focused on violent extremism and social media.
qAndA.question: What are the proposed gun control measures in New York State?

qAndA.answer: Because in most states, including those that require licensing for handguns, there is no licensing requirement for purchasing semi-automatic rifles.
qAndA.question: Why is Senator Stewart-Cousins emphasizing the importance of the new licensing requirement for semi-automatic rifles?

qAndA.answer: Because the Buffalo shooter was active on social media and used the platform to communicate his plans, highlighting the need to address violent extremism and hate speech online.
qAndA.question: Why is the senator calling for accountability for social media platforms?

qAndA.answer: The security guard at Tops Market, a retired police officer, was shot by the perpetrator but was likely not severely injured due to his body armor. This allowed the shooter to continue his attack, making access to body armor a point of concern.
qAndA.question: How might the outlawing of body armor sales to civilians have impacted the Buffalo shooting?

qAndA.answer: While the interview starts with a neutral and informative tone, it becomes increasingly serious and passionate as the senator delves into the specifics of the new laws and the urgency of addressing gun violence.
qAndA.question: What is the overall mood of the interview with Senator Stewart-Cousins?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Well, New York's governor, Kathy Hoekle, announced a package of ten new bills designed to
tighten gun laws across the state.
A lawmaker say they could close loopholes that may have contributed to that mass shooting
at top market in Buffalo last month.
If passed, the legislation would raise the age for buying semi-automatic rifles to 21,
tighten existing red flag laws and ban civilians from buying body armor.
The bills are expected to pass because of the state's Democrat-controlled legislature
and be signed into law later this month.
Joining us now is New York State's Senate Majority Leader, Democrat Andrea Stewart-Cousins.
Senator, thank you so much for being here.
What of these laws would have changed what happened to the tragedy in Buffalo?
Well, again, thank you for having me.
But, you know, I think when we looked at Buffalo, we look at what New York has done, we wish
everything could have changed.
But what we do know is that we have red flag laws.
And we're looking into why they weren't utilized, for example.
People spoke to this young man who had threatened to commit suicide and do a shooting, and yet
he was let go.
So one of the laws that we'll be passing tomorrow will say that there is a responsibility
for the police, for the district attorney, and also there will be an opportunity for
health care providers to be able to apply for these extreme risk protection orders.
I think people want to know that we have laws that could really prevent some of this,
and people should be using them properly.
So I think that would be helpful.
The other thing that we want to make sure is that you have to be 21 or older to get a
semi-automatic rifle.
I mean, there is no reason why we're just having anyone wait to their 18th birthday and
run in and get something that's a weapon of mass destruction.
So we will be changing that law as well.
There will be a licensing process that you cannot really enter into unless you're 21.
We're looking at social media.
I mean, here's a guy, again, apparently in Buffalo, he was on social media.
He was actually telling people that he was planning to do this mass shooting.
And so we've established a department.
We will be establishing through this legislation, a department in the district attorney's office,
that will be able to look at social media, violent extremism, hate speech, and really
trying to have some accountability with the social media platforms so that these things
are not ignored and absolutely followed up on.
So there are a number of things.
We're also doing micro stamping and, by the way, the security guard, the retired police officer,
Mr. Sultar, who shot at the perpetrator of the top's mass shooting, didn't wound him
because he was wearing a vest, body armor.
So what we've done now is we'll be outlawing the sale of body armor because unless you're
law enforcement, military, or there's some other reason, emergency services, et cetera,
that you should be wearing body armor.
We don't necessarily think that's as important for people to just go in and buy vest.
So there are a number of things that we are doing.
Hopefully, we will lead, but I mean, even more hopefully, we will stop this culture of
guns and violence and just not be in a position where we're burying our seniors, we're
burying our children.
We can do much, much better.
Yeah, it's a suite of 10 bills, and I want to zero in on one specifically because I think
a lot of people don't know that most states do not require a license to purchase one of
these semi-automatic rifles or a long gun.
Even states that require licensing for handguns.
And that point alone, it requiring a license to get one of these guns, could go a long
way to keep them out of the hands who do not, who should not have them, speak to that
if you would.
That is exactly right.
I mean, again, these are weapons of mass destruction.
They're weapons of war.
What is the need?
But if you do need this, then you go through a licensing process.
The licensing process will, I mean, if necessary, it'll be a cooling off period of whatever
it is.
And the permitting processing will only be applicable if you're 21 and older.
So I hope that people will think twice about what it is they are doing, and certainly if
they're not thinking twice, we already have background checks.
We've got now this permitting process that's going to have to happen.
We will force them through the process to have the time to think about what exactly they're
planning to do with a weapon of mass destruction.
New York State Senator Andrea Sturtkazen, thank you very much for all the information.
Thank you so much.
